questions.q: What makes modern version control systems such as Git and Mercurial 'distributed'?
options: They do not need a centralised server to host the repository
They split each file across several computers
They only work while connected to the internet
They email every change to all collaborators
questions.explain: Older systems like CVS or Subversion relied on a central server; Git and Mercurial do not.
questions.evidence: meaning that they do not need a centralized server to host the repository

questions.q: Why should you avoid creating a Git repository inside another repository?
options: Git cannot track subdirectories at all
Each subdirectory must have its own .git folder
The inner repository would delete the outer one's history
Nested repositories interfere: the outer one tries to version-control the inner one
questions.explain: One repository already tracks every file and subdirectory below it, so create each new repository in a separate directory.
questions.evidence: the outer repository will try to version-control the inner repository

questions.q: Why does Git keep a file's history in the special .git directory?
options: So files are published to GitHub automatically
To compress files so they take less space
So the filesystem isn't cluttered and old versions can't be edited or deleted by accident
Because the working directory cannot hold text files
questions.explain: Your working files stay clean while every committed version is stored safely inside .git.
questions.evidence: so that our filesystem doesn't become cluttered (and so that we can't accidentally edit or delete an old version)

questions.q: What does the lesson call good practice before saving changes as a commit?
options: Delete the previous commit
Always review the changes first
Push to GitHub before committing
Leave the commit message empty
questions.explain: Reviewing (for example with git diff) catches mistakes before they become part of the history.
questions.evidence: It is good practice to always review our changes before saving them.

questions.q: In Git, what does the identifier HEAD refer to?
options: The most recent commit
The first commit in the repository
The remote repository on GitHub
The file currently open in your editor
questions.explain: HEAD~1 then means the commit before the most recent one.
questions.evidence: which refers to the most recent commit

questions.q: By convention, what name is usually given to the main remote repository?
options: upstream
master
HEAD
origin
questions.explain: The name only exists locally, but origin is the default used by git and GitHub.
questions.evidence: origin is a convention that is often used by default in git and GitHub

questions.q: What is SSH, which the lesson uses to connect to GitHub?
options: A Git command that merges branches
A file format for storing commits
A cryptographic protocol for secure communication over an insecure network
GitHub's web page for pull requests
questions.explain: SSH uses a key pair: a public key you can share and a private key you keep secret.
questions.evidence: SSH is a cryptographic network protocol that allows secure communication between computers using an otherwise insecure network.

questions.q: In a basic collaborative workflow, what should you do before making your own changes?
options: Delete your copy and clone it again
Run git pull to get the latest version
Push your old commits first
Rename the remote repository
questions.explain: Working from the latest version reduces conflicts with your collaborators' changes.
questions.evidence: you should git pull before making our changes

questions.q: When do conflicts occur in Git?
options: When two or more people change the same lines of the same file
Whenever two people edit the same repository
Whenever a file is renamed
When a commit message is too long
questions.explain: Changes to different lines merge automatically; overlapping changes must be resolved by hand.
questions.evidence: Conflicts occur when two or more people change the same lines of the same file.
